items.name: any who out of their simplicity
items.quote: If there be any who out of their simplicity shall say that mettalls are of no use in Physick
items.note: A view the author reports in order to answer it: that metals are useless in physick.

items.quote: created, though not for Mans food yet for his Physick
items.note: The author holds that metals were created for man's physick, not his food.

items.quote: although man partaketh of those Three first
items.note: A group of three is named as 'those Three first', of which man partakes; the paragraph does not spell out which three. Interpreted: the following words name Animall, Vegetable and Minerall.

items.quote: the Animall, Vegetable and Minerall sperm or seed have but one rise or originall, and differ onely in Quality of Place and Receptacle
items.note: The author's answer: the three kinds of seed have one origin and differ only by place and receptacle.

items.name: Theophrast.
items.quote: See Theophrast. his Manuel.
items.note: The margin note names Theophrast. and his Manuel beside the paragraph on metals in physick.

items.quote: since Man hath Physick for his body from the world because he is a world, therefore all Mineralls are for Mans good
items.note: The note gives the reason minerals serve man: man is a world and takes his physick from the world.

items.quote: Animall, Vegetable, and Minerall principles are one and the same in all things, but have various Receptacles
items.note: The three kinds of principle are one; only their receptacles differ.

items.quote: which is the generall seed of all things or subject of the first matter
items.note: The text glosses the 'most principall and generall principall kind' as the general seed of all things, the subject of the first matter.

items.quote: from which Nature hath the nature of Quick-silver to create every other Compound
items.note: From this general kind Nature takes 'the nature of Quick-silver' to make every compound.

items.quote: All things are from one Principle, and tendeth to one
items.note: One principle as origin and end of all things.

items.name: Orpheus
items.quote: In Orpheus his Night
items.note: Orpheus's Night is cited as a name for the one in which all things are.

items.name: Hippocrates
items.quote: Hippocrates his river Orcus
items.note: Hippocrates's river Orcus is cited for the same one.

items.name: Anaxagoras
items.quote: like Anaxagoras his Pamsperm
items.note: Anaxagoras's Pamsperm is set beside them as a like name for the one.

items.quote: which Aristotle unjustly condemned
items.note: The author judges Aristotle's condemnation of the Pamsperm unjust; the following words say Aristotle did not understand it.

items.quote: which Nature is the Specifick of every Creature
items.note: The one Nature, 'the Essence and Matter of all things', is said to be the Specifick of every creature.

items.quote: according to the agitation and operation of the Universall spirit
items.note: Bodies come forth varied by place and receptacle and by the working of the Universall spirit.

items.quote: This is the set Order for the government of the sublunary Family
items.what: the set Order for the government of the sublunary Family
items.note: Named order: minerals nourish vegetables, vegetables beasts, beasts men.

items.quote: which could not be if the nature of one thing did not by affinity partake of the nature of another
items.note: The feeding chain rests on affinity of natures, reaching back to the first kind.

items.quote: Thus also the Spirit of life is united through out the whole body of man, but is various according to parts of the body in which it is.
items.note: The note sets a parallel in man's body: one spirit of life, varied by the part it is in.

items.quote: All things flow from one Fountaine, which after they have done their work and quitted the Stage of Vanity, are returned to their own places
items.note: All things come from one fountain and return to their places at rest.

items.quote: That universall Spirit which liveth in and quickneth this whole Masse, which worketh all in all, and filleth the whole world
items.note: The text says what the universall Spirit does: lives in and quickens the whole mass and fills the world; it is also called 'that Power of God'.

items.name: Agrippa
items.quote: Agrippa calleth it the subject of all mirability, the Ens or Being that cannot be comprehended by sence
items.note: Agrippa's name for the universal spirit.

items.name: Avicen
items.quote: Avicen saith, it is the Soule of the world powred into all things
items.note: Avicen's name for it: the Soul of the world.

items.name: Plato, the Arabians and Caldeans
items.quote: building on the authority of Plato, the Arabians and Caldeans
items.note: Avicen's saying is said to rest on these authorities.

items.quote: but this we must hearken to without any superstition or Idolatrous worship, giving honour onely to One God
items.note: The author limits how these sayings are to be received: no idolatry, honour to God alone.

items.name: Rom. 8.
items.quote: Rom. 8.
items.note: The margin note names Rom. 8 beside the paragraph on the universal spirit.

items.name: Paracelsus
items.quote: See Paracelsus his Apocalyps of Herines.
items.note: The note points to Paracelsus's Apocalyps of Herines beside the same paragraph.

items.quote: The Soule of the world is a kind of united life, filling, gathering and knitting together all things
items.note: The note says what the Soul of the world is.

items.quote: infusing into them occult qualities which are commonly called the Fift Effences
items.note: Occult qualities infused into things are said to be commonly called the Fift Effences (spelling as given).

items.quote: is the invisible Fire or fiery vigour by which all things are multiplyed
items.note: Nature, 'the Image of God' (one letter illegible), is said to be the invisible fire by which all things multiply.

items.quote: Nature many times makes it selfe merry with its magistery or mastership
items.note: Magistery is glossed as mastership.

items.quote: Nature, I say, is that medium which by an Harmonicall consent joyneth the lowest things to the highest
items.note: The author defines Nature as the medium joining lowest to highest.

items.quote: sometimes is called Animall, sometimes Vegetable, sometimes Minerall, according to the diversity of the subject or receptacle
items.note: The same Nature takes the three names by its receptacle.

items.quote: the three Families of Nature
items.note: The three kinds are named as families of Nature.

items.quote: that Silesiac child in our age, which was born though not with a golden yet with a gilded tooth in the left and lower jaw, which I did both see and handle
items.note: The author's own witness, at Prague, of a child with a gilded tooth, as an example of Nature's work.

items.quote: the Hermetick Phylosophy
items.note: A named philosophy whose seekers are not astonished at such works.

items.quote: for it is not unlawfull to pry into those things which exceed even naturall order
items.note: The author holds it lawful to search what exceeds natural order.

items.quote: from the intimacy of more hid and secret Phylosophy
items.note: A 'hid and secret' philosophy is the source of what these seekers know.

items.quote: that same Spirit and minerall Nature which produceth Gold in the bowells of the Earth is also in Man
items.note: The gold-making spirit of the earth is said to be in man.

items.quote: That Spirit in Gold is the same with the generating spirit of all Creatures
items.note: The spirit in gold equals the generating spirit of all creatures; it has 'assumed a Naturall body' and rules Nature.

items.name: Albertus Magnus
items.quote: Albertus Magnus writeth, that in his time there hath been Gold found in the bodyes and heads of some that were hanged
items.note: Albertus's report of gold found in bodies.

items.name: Albertus Magnus
items.quote: There is not, saith he, that thing Elementated of the four Elements in which Gold Naturally may not be found in the last subtiliation thereof.
items.note: Quoted from his Book of Mineralls: gold is in every elementated thing at its last subtiliation.

items.name: the Phylosophers
items.quote: the Phylosophers say that the matter of their Mystery may be had every where, because it consisteth in every Elementated thing
items.note: The Phylosophers' saying that the matter of their Mystery is everywhere.

items.quote: the matter of their Mystery
items.note: The philosophers' work is named a Mystery and its matter set apart as one thing.

items.name: Albertus
items.quote: Albertus also proveth, that the greatest Minerall vertue is in every Man, but especially in the head among the teeth
items.note: Albertus on mineral virtue in man, with gold found among teeth in graves.

items.quote: which could not be if there were not a minerall vertue in Man, which minerall vertue is in the Elixer of Phylosophers
items.note: Whose inference this is the text does not show (UNCLEAR: Albertus's or the author's); it ties the mineral virtue in man to the Elixer of Phylosophers.

items.name: Albertus
items.quote: In his Mineralls.
items.note: The note names Albertus's Mineralls as the source.

items.quote: King Calid who inquired after the matter of the Elixer
items.note: The matter of the Elixer is the thing asked after.

items.name: Morienes
items.quote: It is of thee O King, said he,
items.note: Morienes, called 'Chymiologer', answers that the matter is of the king; the next words add 'thou are in its Mine'.

items.name: Raymund Lully
items.quote: he got his matter out of a mean and worthlesse thing
items.note: Lully's saying that his matter came from a mean thing.

items.quote: Wherein he never a jot differed from Raymund Lully
items.note: The author judges Morienes and Lully to agree.

items.quote: Lullius was a divine & most compleat Phylosopher, whom Paracel. blamed without a cause.
items.note: The note praises Lullius and says Paracel. blamed him without cause.

items.quote: in natural things, which is calld the Vegetall Spirit
items.note: The first mover in natural things (one letter illegible) is called the Vegetall Spirit.

items.quote: by whom our matter of a stone goeth beyond the rest
items.note: The note names 'our matter of a stone' and says this spirit is in animals, vegetables and minerals.

items.name: Riplaeus à Portis
items.quote: Remember that Man is the most noble Creature of all, in whom there is the Naturall Mercuriality of the four Elements
items.note: Riplaeus: man holds the natural Mercuriality of the elements.

items.name: Riplaeus à Portis
items.quote: which is of little worth, and may be got out of its Mine by art
items.note: That thing is of little worth and is got from its mine by art.

items.name: Rhasis
items.quote: in every thing there is every thing potentially, though it doth not actually appear
items.note: From Rhasis's Book of Divinity: all things are in each thing potentially, unseen.

items.quote: not by common and outside arguments, but by solyd reasons drawn from the inside of things
items.note: The author says the philosophers confirm these things by reasons from the inside of things.

items.quote: But these things are by the by.
items.what: these things are by the by
items.note: The author marks the run of authorities as a digression.

items.quote: The Chymicall way of Subtiliating Extracting, and Separating
items.what: The Chymicall way of Subtiliating Extracting, and Separating
items.note: The chemical way is named by three operations; said to be unknown to Galen.

items.quote: for they knew not how to separate the bark and husk from the kernell
items.note: The ancients' lack is put as not separating bark and husk from kernel, the image of the chapter heading.

items.name: Galen
items.quote: that he tryed all wayes and means to distinguish the facultyes of simple medicines, and discern the hot parts of vineger from the cold
items.note: Galen's own words on seeking to separate the parts of vinegar and milk.

items.quote: who in this thing might have obtained his desire if he had been well skild in the Distillatory Art
items.note: The author: the Distillatory Art would have given Galen what he sought.

items.name: Galen
items.quote: Lib. 1. cap. 19.
items.note: The note gives the place in Galen's book for the quoted words.

items.quote: Whey, Butter and Cheese are the three first things of milk, for all Terresterity is Salt.
items.note: The note names the three first things of milk.

items.quote: which is the order and series of Gods works, and obey the power, word and command of God
items.note: Nature is glossed as the order and series of God's works.

items.quote: doe communicate particular gifts to severall ages
items.note: God and Nature give particular gifts to different ages, so the ancients' ignorance is no disgrace.

items.quote: Doubtlesse if Galen had lived when Paracelsus did, he would not have envyed, but reverenced his learning
items.note: The author's judgement of how Galen would have met Paracelsus; the sentence goes on to say Galen would have served 'Theophraestus'. Interpreted: the sentence uses both names for one man.

items.quote: to separate the three first (qualities) in vineger
items.note: The three first of vinegar are named as things to separate; 'qualities' stands in brackets.

items.quote: to learn the preparations of those high Magisteryes and Elixirs
items.note: The preparations of magisteries and elixirs are named as the chief thing to learn.

items.quote: neither would he have refufed to blow the coals or temper his stuffe, or watch his work
items.note: The labour of the work: blowing coals, tempering the stuff, watching the work.

items.quote: who have not learned so much as their A. B. C. in the Spagyrick Physick
items.note: The author's charge against the Philerastian physicians.

items.quote: the Creation and composition of the internall Astrall Man, much lesse of the Mechanick Spirits of diseases
items.what: the internall Astrall Man; the Mechanick Spirits of diseases
items.note: Two named objects of knowledge the opponents lack.

items.name: Philerastian Physitians
items.quote: whom these men fear not to call a circumforaneous or rambling rayler, one that was no Phylosopher at all
items.note: The opponents' words about Paracelsus, reported to be rejected.

items.quote: that never sufficiently commended Paracelsus, a thousand-fold more worthy then his adversaries, and the immortall glory of Germany
items.note: The author's praise of Paracelsus.

items.quote: who had the absolute knowledge of all Divine and Humane sciences
items.note: The author ascribes to Paracelsus absolute knowledge of all sciences.

items.quote: We have all our faylings, happy is he that hath least
items.note: The author answers attacks on Paracelsus's life by common failings.

items.quote: his human imperfections which none will excuse, they should have born with the like tendernes of compassion where with they pardon Galens impiety
items.note: Paracelsus's faults should be borne as Galen's impiety is pardoned.

items.quote: Galens impiety who scoffed at the doctrin of Moses & Christ
items.note: The author charges Galen with scoffing at Moses and Christ.

items.name: Galen
items.quote: In his second Book of the difference of Pulses.
items.note: The note gives the place in Galen for the charge of impiety.

items.quote: Doubtles he would have more clearly have manifested to thankful posterity his Secrets which God disclosed to him, and written more plainly and perfectly of Preparations
items.note: Theophrastus is said to have written his secrets and preparations less plainly than he would have for a thankful age.

items.quote: by being againe put to seek out the certainty and truth of that which Theophrastus discoursed and writ of
items.note: The present Spagyrick profession must seek out again what Theophrastus wrote.

items.quote: that there are so few to be found who have the true medicines prepared according to Theophrastus his minde, of which he treateth at large in his Books
items.note: Few have the true medicines prepared as Theophrastus meant.

items.name: Paracelsus
items.quote: See Paracelsus in Paragr.
items.note: The note points to Paracelsus 'in Paragr.' beside this passage.

items.quote: for they require solutions, mortifications, cohibitions, resuscitations, &c. truly Phylosophycall
items.note: The steps the true medicines require; the list is left open with '&c.'.

items.quote: which cannot be understood without true Physick
items.note: These steps need true physick, and (after the note mark) astronomy and chymistry.

items.quote: nor are they compleated in a short time, but with much tediousnesse to Phylosophists who are impatient of delay
items.note: The work takes long; 'Phylosophists' are impatient of it.

items.name: Paracelsus
items.quote: A Physitian must be an Astronomer, otherwise Paracelsus saith that his Physick is but imposture and a cheat.
items.note: Paracelsus's saying on the physician as astronomer.

items.quote: Therefore many with Icarus are drowned in a great Sea.
items.note: A figure: those lacking astronomy fall like Icarus; the note does not say it plainly.

items.quote: But truly I think this wicked generation is not worthy of such medicines.
items.note: The author's own judgement on his age.

items.quote: his mighty and marvellous works from unworthy Men
items.note: God withholds his works from the unworthy; a word before it is in foreign script and not given.

items.quote: He will never suffer those Secrets to be known, especially in these corrupt and perilous times
items.note: The secrets are withheld in these times.

items.quote: almost all men have a burning desire after making Gold
items.note: Most seek gold-making and neglect the preparation of medicines.

items.quote: the onely cause thereof is their not knowing the Metaphysicks of Paracelsus, the true Phylosophy
items.note: The cause named: ignorance of Paracelsus's Metaphysicks.

items.name: Theophrastus
items.quote: those large Books which Theophrastus directeth unto in his Labyrinth of Physitians
items.note: Theophrastus's Labyrinth of Physitians directs to books to be read first.

items.quote: before they set upon the preparations, separations and resolution of Naturall things
items.note: The steps of work, to come only after that reading.

items.quote: There are four Pillars of Physick, Phylosophy, Alchymistry, Astronomy, and the Physicall vertue or medicine.
items.note: The note names and numbers four pillars.

items.quote: most Chymists betake themselves to Court, and are turned from the truth by the glitter of Court-service
items.note: The author's complaint that court service turns chymists from the truth.

items.quote: many have begun well, but deluded with these toyes, have made an ill end
items.note: His own observation over many years.

items.quote: this Divine Spagyrie, the most wonderfull and approved Art
items.note: The art is named and praised; said to be disparaged by the ruder sort.

items.quote: the bettter the thing is, the more destructive is the abuse of it
items.note: Abuse does not condemn a good art.

items.name: the Athenian Thrasos
items.quote: the Athenian Thrasos who will have Light to be Darkenesse, and Darkenesse to be Light
items.note: Opponents named as the Athenian Thrasos, whose view is reported to be rejected.

items.quote: For the world seeketh not the Truth but its own Honour
items.note: The author's judgement on the world, followed by God giving it up to a reprobate sense.

items.quote: for as yet the Invention of Arts hath not attained the utmost end
items.note: The arts are not yet complete.

items.quote: confute the delusions and errours of the schoolmen not with words, but deeds; not Syllogistically, but Really and indeed
items.note: The author hopes the schoolmen will be refuted by deeds, not syllogisms.

items.quote: the time of Revocation and Regeneration drawing nigh
items.what: the time of Revocation and Regeneration
items.note: A coming time is named, when the imperfect comes to nought.

items.quote: who suffer the Old man to be ruled by the Sydereall Spirit
items.note: Pride of titles is tied to the Old man ruled by the Sydereall Spirit.

items.quote: deliver them from the chaines of Utter Darknesse and incessant janglings of Putatitious and conceited Schollers
items.note: The chapter ends in prayer against conceited scholars.
